claim: Human tactile afferents provide essential feedback for grasp stability during dexterous object manipulation.
source: Human tactile afferents provide essential feedback for grasp stability during dexterous object manipulation.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that draws from established understanding in the field of tactile neuroscience.

claim: Interacting forces between an object and the fingers induce slip events that are thought to provide information about grasp stability.
source: Interacting forces between an object and the fingers induce slip events that are thought to provide information about grasp stability.
evidence: This statement reflects established understanding in the field, indicated by 'are thought to provide'.

claim: All afferents were sensitive to slip events.
source: We found that all afferents were sensitive to slip events, but fast-adapting type I (FA-I) afferents in particular faithfully encoded compressive strain rates resulting from those slips.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Fast-adapting type I (FA-I) afferents faithfully encoded compressive strain rates resulting from slip events.
source: We found that all afferents were sensitive to slip events, but fast-adapting type I (FA-I) afferents in particular faithfully encoded compressive strain rates resulting from those slips.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: FA-I afferents are well suited to detect incipient slips given their high density in fingerpads.
source: Given the high density of FA-I afferents in fingerpads, they are well suited to detect incipient slips and to provide essential information for the control of grip force during manipulation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings combined with known anatomical facts about FA-I afferent density.

claim: FA-I afferents provide essential information for the control of grip force during manipulation.
source: Given the high density of FA-I afferents in fingerpads, they are well suited to detect incipient slips and to provide essential information for the control of grip force during manipulation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings about FA-I responses to slip events.

claim: Humans can quickly and accurately adapt to changes in friction.
source: Previous work has suggested that humans can quickly and accurately adapt to changes in friction (Westling and Johansson, 1984; Cadoret and Smith, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Tactile feedback is necessary for grip adjustments to take place.
source: Importantly, tactile feedback is necessary for grip adjustments to take place as disruption of this feedback abolishes the normal, fine-tuned grasp control and results in frequent object dropping despite excessive compensatory grip forces (Westling and Johansson, 1987; Augurelle et al., 2003; Witney et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous experimental studies.

claim: Disruption of tactile feedback abolishes normal, fine-tuned grasp control and results in frequent object dropping despite excessive compensatory grip forces.
source: Importantly, tactile feedback is necessary for grip adjustments to take place as disruption of this feedback abolishes the normal, fine-tuned grasp control and results in frequent object dropping despite excessive compensatory grip forces (Westling and Johansson, 1987; Augurelle et al., 2003; Witney et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous experimental studies.

claim: Small, short-lasting slips occur during manipulation.
source: There is indeed evidence that small, short-lasting slips occur during manipulation (Johansson and Westling, 1984).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Small slips trigger strong afferent responses and elicit grip force adjustments.
source: Those slips trigger strong afferent responses and elicit grip force adjustments (Johansson and Westling, 1987).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Tactile slip is not instantaneous but develops progressively.
source: Tactile slip is not instantaneous but develops progressively (Levesque and Hayward, 2003; Tada et al., 2006; André et al., 2011; Terekhov and Hayward, 2011; Delhaye et al., 2014; Barrea et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: As surface-tangential force increases, local slips begin at the periphery of the contact and progress toward the center until full slip occurs.
source: As the surface-tangential force, that is, traction, of the fingerpad increases, 'local' slips begin at the periphery of the contact and progress toward the center until the last central 'stuck' point finally slips, that is, the instant of a 'full slip' or a global slip.
evidence: This is a description of the slip phenomenon based on established knowledge and previous work.

claim: The partial slip phase gives rise to substantial local strain patterns in the slipping regions near the boundary between stuck and slipping points.
source: Such a phenomenon gives rise to substantial local strain patterns in the slipping regions, near the boundary between the stuck and the slipping points (Delhaye et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Type I afferents respond strongly to local skin deformation.
source: Single-unit recordings of primary tactile afferents, both in humans and monkeys, have shown that type I afferents respond strongly to local skin deformation (Johansson et al., 1982; Sripati et al., 2006; Saal et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Type I afferent responses contain information about local geometric features such as edge orientation.
source: Those responses contain information about local geometric features such as edge orientation (Pruszynski and Johansson, 2014; Suresh et al., 2016; Delhaye et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Afferents of all types in hairy skin strongly respond to local skin stretch.
source: Afferent recordings in the hairy skin of the human hand have shown that afferents of all types strongly respond to local skin stretch and that the fast-adapting type I (FA-I) afferents also strongly respond when the stretch is released (Edin, 1992; Edin, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: FA-I afferents in hairy skin strongly respond when stretch is released.
source: Afferent recordings in the hairy skin of the human hand have shown that afferents of all types strongly respond to local skin stretch and that the fast-adapting type I (FA-I) afferents also strongly respond when the stretch is released (Edin, 1992; Edin, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: SA-II afferents are sensitive to skin stretch.
source: Slowly-adapting type II (SA-II) afferents are also known to be sensitive to skin stretch, but relating their response to the exact local stretch pattern is complex given the large size of their receptive fields.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SA-II afferents.

claim: Relating SA-II afferent response to exact local stretch pattern is complex due to their large receptive fields.
source: Slowly-adapting type II (SA-II) afferents are also known to be sensitive to skin stretch, but relating their response to the exact local stretch pattern is complex given the large size of their receptive fields.
evidence: This is an inference based on known anatomical properties of SA-II afferents.

claim: How glabrous skin afferents respond to local skin strain has never been studied.
source: How glabrous skin afferents, that is, those engaged in the contact with objects during manipulation, respond to local skin strain has, to our knowledge, never been studied.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature at the time of the study.

claim: All tactile afferents in the fingertip responded to slip events.
source: We found that all tactile afferents in the fingertip responded to slip events, but that FA-I afferents in particular faithfully signaled local skin compressions related to the progression of slips.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: FA-I afferents faithfully signaled local skin compressions related to the progression of slips.
source: We found that all tactile afferents in the fingertip responded to slip events, but that FA-I afferents in particular faithfully signaled local skin compressions related to the progression of slips.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: FA-I afferents are primarily responsible for detecting changes in surface strains.
source: We suggest that FA-I afferents are primarily responsible for detecting changes in surface strains and that their discharges are a primary source of information for the central nervous system to, for instance, quickly adjust fingertip forces to different levels of friction.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: FA-I afferent discharges are a primary source of information for the central nervous system to quickly adjust fingertip forces to different levels of friction.
source: We suggest that FA-I afferents are primarily responsible for detecting changes in surface strains and that their discharges are a primary source of information for the central nervous system to, for instance, quickly adjust fingertip forces to different levels of friction.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: The transparent plate exerted a servo-controlled normal force of 4 N.
source: The plate exerted a servo-controlled normal force of 4 N and was moved tangentially in one of four directions (U: ulnar; D: distal; R: radial; P: proximal).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: The plate was moved tangentially in one of four directions: ulnar, distal, radial, and proximal.
source: The plate exerted a servo-controlled normal force of 4 N and was moved tangentially in one of four directions (U: ulnar; D: distal; R: radial; P: proximal).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Strain waves started moving at the onset of movement from opposite sides and from the periphery of the contact toward the center and disappeared at the point of full slip.
source: Those waves started moving at the onset of movement from opposite sides and from the periphery of the contact toward the center and disappeared at the point of full slip (Delhaye et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data, with a citation to previous work.

claim: Once full slip was reached, the changes in strain faded away.
source: Once the full slip was reached, the changes in strain faded away.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Different movement directions elicited different strain patterns at all points in the contact area.
source: Different movement directions elicited different patterns (i.e., compression, stretch, or shear) at all points in the contact area.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Sufficient recordings for data analysis were obtained from 22 afferents (13 FA-I, 6 SA-I, 2 SA-II, and 1 FA-II).
source: Sufficient recordings for data analysis (three out of five repetitions of each plate move direction) were obtained from 22 afferents (13 FA-I, 6 SA-I, 2 SA-II, and 1 FA-II).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental data collected.

claim: FA-I units showed a phasic response, with a burst of activity at the instant of contact and another one during tangential loading.
source: FA-I units showed a phasic response, with a burst of activity at the instant of contact, and another one during the tangential loading (e.g., Figure 2A).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data, with reference to Figure 2A.

claim: A majority of FA-I afferents responded mostly only during the partial slip phase, showing no or almost no response during the onset and plateau phases.
source: However, a majority of FA-I afferents responded mostly only during the partial slip phase, showing no or almost no response during the start ('onset' phase) and the end ('plateau' phase) of the tangential movement (for U115-04 in Figure 2A, there was one spike at the onset phase during one repeat).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data, with reference to Figure 2A.

claim: SA-I units presented a rather tonic response beginning at the initial contact that changed during the tangential loading phase by increasing or decreasing their firing rates.
source: SA-I units instead presented a rather tonic response beginning at the initial contact that changed during the tangential loading phase by increasing or decreasing their firing rates (e.g., Figure 2C).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data, with reference to Figure 2C.

claim: The tangential movement of the plate led to slight fluctuations in the normal force that could not be suppressed by the force controller.
source: Note that the tangential movement of the plate led to slight fluctuations in the normal force that could not be suppressed by the force controller (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a description of a limitation in the experimental setup.

claim: Normal force fluctuations did not evoke strong afferent responses.
source: Those fluctuations did not evoke strong afferent responses.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Discharge rates were neither correlated to the normal force nor to its derivative.
source: Indeed, the discharge rates were neither correlated to the normal force nor to its derivative (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: For all four afferent types, the fraction of trials during which the afferent responded with at least one spike was higher for the partial slip phase than for the two other phases.
source: Indeed, for all four afferent types, the fraction of trials during which the afferent responded with at least one spike was higher for the partial slip phase than for the two others (one-way ANOVA with repeated measures, F(2,24) = 47.05, p<0.001 for FA-I units; F(2,10) = 13.97, p=0.001 for SA-I units; all p<0.05 for paired comparisons; for FA-II and SA-II afferents, we did not have enough data for such analysis).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: FA-I units were silent during the plateau phase, except when a stick-and-slip phenomenon was observed.
source: FA-I units were silent during the plateau, except when a stick-and-slip phenomenon was observed, in which case the firing phase was locked to the stick-and-slip events (e.g., see U109-04 during plateau phase in Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data, with reference to a figure.

claim: Different movement directions elicited different responses in afferents.
source: We found that different movement directions elicited different responses, confirming previous observations (Birznieks et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data that confirms previous work.

claim: Some FA-I units tended to have a preferred-opposite pattern (5 out of 13).
source: Some FA-I units tended to have a preferred-opposite pattern (5 out of 13), that is, the preferred ('N' for North in Figure 3B) and opposite directions ('S' for South in 3B) tended to elicit a stronger response than the two other directions.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: The distribution of the preferred global direction covered the four directions tested with a slight preference for the proximal-distal axis.
source: The distribution of the preferred global direction covered the four directions tested; however, we observed overall a slight preference for the proximal-distal axis (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: Firing rates during partial slips were consistent across forward and backward movements.
source: Firing rates during partial slips were consistent across forward and backward (Figure 3D; correlation r = 0.97, n = 176, p<0.001), suggesting similar directional preference when the skin was already under tension (backward movement).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: Firing rates were strongly correlated across friction levels.
source: While the firing rates were strongly correlated across friction levels (Figure 3E; correlation r = 0.95, n = 176, p<0.001), the firing rates across the whole population tended to be slightly lower for low friction (paired t-test, t(171) = 7.57, p<0.001) and the ratio of the mean firing rate during low and high friction condition was 0.82 ± 0.55 (mean ± std).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: Firing rates across the whole population tended to be slightly lower for low friction.
source: While the firing rates were strongly correlated across friction levels (Figure 3E; correlation r = 0.95, n = 176, p<0.001), the firing rates across the whole population tended to be slightly lower for low friction (paired t-test, t(171) = 7.57, p<0.001) and the ratio of the mean firing rate during low and high friction condition was 0.82 ± 0.55 (mean ± std).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The discharge of FA-I units was strongly coupled to the compressive strain changes taking place in their receptive fields during the partial slip phase.
source: We observed that the discharge of FA-I units was strongly coupled to the compressive strain changes taking place in their receptive fields during the partial slip phase (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: The low friction surface exhibited full slip at a lower level of tangential force and earlier than the high friction surface.
source: Moreover, the low friction surface exhibited full slip at a lower level of tangential force, and therefore also earlier than the high friction surface, with respect to the movement onset.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The response evoked by a stretch wave was much weaker than its compressive counterpart.
source: Finally, we observed that the response evoked by a stretch wave, generated by a distal movement (Figure 4A, right, and B, left), was much weaker than its compressive counterpart.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The timing of the response was perfectly synchronized with the occurrence of the stretch in the receptive field.
source: Still, the timing of the response was perfectly synchronized with the occurrence of the stretch in the receptive field.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The average strains causing spikes in all recorded FA-I afferents had a clear, more or less annular (ring-like) pattern.
source: We found that, indeed, the average strains causing spikes in all recorded FA-I afferents had a clear, more or less annular (ring-like) pattern (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a finding from the spike-triggered average analysis.

claim: The annular pattern overlapped the afferent's receptive field and often peaked inside it.
source: Importantly, however, the pattern overlapped the afferent's receptive field and often peaked inside it.
evidence: This is an observation from the spike-triggered average analysis.

claim: Clear patterns did not emerge for the SA-I afferents in the spike-triggered average analysis.
source: Strikingly, clear patterns did not emerge for the SA-I afferents, suggesting that those afferents are less sensitive to the local surface strain changes (Figure 5A, bottom).
evidence: This is a finding from the spike-triggered average analysis.

claim: SA-I afferents are less sensitive to local surface strain changes.
source: Strikingly, clear patterns did not emerge for the SA-I afferents, suggesting that those afferents are less sensitive to the local surface strain changes (Figure 5A, bottom).
evidence: This is an inference from the spike-triggered average analysis.

claim: The compressive STA peaks were generally larger and more often found in the afferent receptive field than their tensile counterpart.
source: Moreover, we found that the compressive STA peaks were generally larger and more often found in the afferent receptive field than their tensile counterpart, suggesting that FA-I afferents are more sensitive to compression.
evidence: This is a finding from the spike-triggered average analysis using principal strain components.

claim: FA-I afferents are more sensitive to compression than to stretch.
source: Moreover, we found that the compressive STA peaks were generally larger and more often found in the afferent receptive field than their tensile counterpart, suggesting that FA-I afferents are more sensitive to compression.
evidence: This is an inference from the spike-triggered average analysis.

claim: The linear model could predict the discharge pattern of the FA-I afferents, but not the SA-I afferents.
source: The results obtained using the model-based approach revealed similar trends as the first model-free method. The linear model could predict the discharge pattern of the FA-I afferents, but not the SA-I afferents.
evidence: This is a finding from the linear regression modeling analysis.

claim: FA-I afferents respond to local strain patterns generated during partial slips.
source: In summary, we observed that FA-I afferents respond to local strain patterns generated during partial slips.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experimental data analyses.

claim: The compressive principal component always outperformed the tensile one in predicting FA-I afferent responses.
source: However, we found that the compressive principal component always outperformed the tensile one, suggesting that the afferents are more sensitive to compression than to stretch.
evidence: This is a finding from the model comparison analysis.

claim: FA-I afferents are more sensitive to compression than to stretch.
source: However, we found that the compressive principal component always outperformed the tensile one, suggesting that the afferents are more sensitive to compression than to stretch.
evidence: This is an inference from the model comparison analysis.

claim: FA-I afferents did not respond to compression in any orientation but rather to compression along a certain preferred strain orientation.
source: Second, FA-I afferents did not respond to compression in any orientation but rather to compression along a certain preferred strain orientation.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the orientation-dependent model analysis.

claim: Models with one single component along its preferred strain orientation performed as well as the full model comprising all the components.
source: and (2) models with one single component along its preferred strain orientation performed as well as the full model comprising all the components, suggesting that this component is mainly responsible for driving the afferent response.
evidence: This is a finding from the model comparison analysis.

claim: A single strain component along the preferred orientation is mainly responsible for driving the FA-I afferent response.
source: and (2) models with one single component along its preferred strain orientation performed as well as the full model comprising all the components, suggesting that this component is mainly responsible for driving the afferent response.
evidence: This is an inference from the model comparison analysis.

claim: The FA-I afferents' preferred strain orientation seemed to coincide with the local fingerprint orientation.
source: Note that the FA-I afferents' preferred strain orientation seemed to coincide with the local fingerprint orientation, but more data is needed to confirm this trend (Figure 2—figure supplement 2, correlation r = 0.74, p=0.10, n = 6).
evidence: This is a tentative observation from the data analysis, noted as requiring more data for confirmation.

claim: FA-I afferents are sensitive to local skin strains, more so to changes in compressive strain than tensile strain, and respond maximally along a preferred strain orientation.
source: In sum, our analyses strongly suggest that the FA-I are sensitive to local skin strains, more so to changes in compressive strain than tensile strain and that they respond maximally along a preferred strain orientation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from multiple analyses.

claim: Correlations with tangential (horizontal) forces were high for slowly-adapting afferents (SA-I and SA-II), especially for those not inside the contact area.
source: However, the correlations with tangential (horizontal) forces were high for slowly-adapting afferents (SA-I and SA-II), especially for those not inside the contact area (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the correlation analysis.

claim: SA-I and SA-II firing rates were not related to the small vertical (normal) force fluctuations.
source: Their firing rates were however not related to the small vertical (normal) force fluctuations.
evidence: This is a finding from the correlation analysis.

claim: Local compression induced by partial slip generates strong responses from FA-I but not SA-I units.
source: Specifically, the results from our analyses imply that the local compression induced by partial slip generates strong responses from FA-I but not SA-I units.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental data analyses.

claim: FA-I afferents from the fingertip are mostly silent when the fingerpad is stuck to the object and even at the onset and offset of the plate movement.
source: Given that the FA-I from the fingertip are mostly silent when the fingerpad is stuck to the object and even at the onset and offset of the plate movement, their vigorous responses to the changes in compressive strain provide a particularly salient signal that enables contact stability.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: FA-I vigorous responses to changes in compressive strain provide a particularly salient signal that enables contact stability.
source: Given that the FA-I from the fingertip are mostly silent when the fingerpad is stuck to the object and even at the onset and offset of the plate movement, their vigorous responses to the changes in compressive strain provide a particularly salient signal that enables contact stability.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental observations.

claim: FA-I afferents constitute more than 50% of all afferents in the glabrous skin of human fingertips.
source: It is reasonable to suspect that FA-I afferents play a crucial role in maintaining grasp stability since they constitute more than 50% of all afferents in the glabrous skin of a human fingertips (Johansson and Vallbo, 1979).
evidence: This is a fact from the literature, supported by a citation.

claim: FA-I afferents play a crucial role in maintaining grasp stability.
source: It is reasonable to suspect that FA-I afferents play a crucial role in maintaining grasp stability since they constitute more than 50% of all afferents in the glabrous skin of a human fingertips (Johansson and Vallbo, 1979).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings and known anatomical facts.

claim: While partial slips give rise to strong responses, the friction per se is poorly encoded by FA-I.
source: Our results show that while partial slips give rise to strong responses, the friction per se is poorly encoded by FA-I.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental data analyses.

claim: Cortical somatosensory neurons are strong edge detectors.
source: Finally, given that cortical somatosensory neurons are strong edge detectors (DiCarlo et al., 1998; Delhaye et al., 2018), the particularly salient signal from the FA-I afferents will likely be amplified downstream.
evidence: This is a fact from the literature, supported by citations.

claim: The particularly salient signal from the FA-I afferents will likely be amplified downstream in cortical somatosensory neurons.
source: Finally, given that cortical somatosensory neurons are strong edge detectors (DiCarlo et al., 1998; Delhaye et al., 2018), the particularly salient signal from the FA-I afferents will likely be amplified downstream.
evidence: This is a speculation based on known properties of cortical neurons and the experimental findings.

claim: Information about grip safety is present in the response of local tactile afferents at the level of a population of afferents, irrespective of the level of friction.
source: A previous study showed that information about grip safety, that is, the increment of tangential force needed to reach full slip, is present in the response of local tactile afferents at the level of a population of afferents, irrespective of the level of friction (Khamis et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a fact from the literature, supported by a citation.

claim: A linear combination of multiple FA-I units can provide a good estimate of the grip safety.
source: Given that all afferents respond to progressing slips, and that the timing of each FA-I afferent's burst is dependent on how far from the center of contact the afferent is, it is not surprising that a linear combination of multiple FA-I units can provide a good estimate of the grip safety.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings and previous work.

claim: The use of two different frictions allowed disambiguation of the relative contribution of external force and local strain measurements to the afferent response.
source: By using the same protocol with two different frictions, we were able to disambiguate the relative contribution of the external force and the local strain measurements to the afferent response.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design rationale.

claim: Until an instant very close to full slip in the low friction condition, the low and high friction materials lead to very similar normal and tangential force profiles.
source: Indeed, until an instant very close to full slip in the low friction condition, the low and high friction materials lead to very similar normal and tangential force profiles, whereas the surface strain patterns inside the contact area have different timing and their progressions differ very early on.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Surface strain patterns inside the contact area have different timing and their progressions differ very early on between low and high friction conditions.
source: Indeed, until an instant very close to full slip in the low friction condition, the low and high friction materials lead to very similar normal and tangential force profiles, whereas the surface strain patterns inside the contact area have different timing and their progressions differ very early on.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The earlier afferent response in the case of low friction cannot be attributed to the change in tangential force itself.
source: Thanks to this contrast, uniquely provided by the difference in friction, the earlier afferent response in the case of the low friction cannot be attributed to the change in tangential force itself.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental design and data analysis.

claim: Afferent responses, particularly the FA-I units, are related to local slip and are poor predictors of friction per se.
source: The fact that the afferent responses, particularly the FA-I units, are related to local slip and are therefore poor predictors of friction per se suggests that humans could be exquisitely sensitive to detect slip while being poor at estimating friction.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Humans could be exquisitely sensitive to detect slip while being poor at estimating friction.
source: The fact that the afferent responses, particularly the FA-I units, are related to local slip and are therefore poor predictors of friction per se suggests that humans could be exquisitely sensitive to detect slip while being poor at estimating friction.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the experimental findings.

claim: Estimating friction would require the occurrence of partial slips, and the absence of slips would make such estimates impossible.
source: That is, estimating friction would require the occurrence of partial slips, and the absence of slips would make such estimates impossible.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the experimental findings.

claim: The FA-I afferent responses were best predicted by compressive strain, rather than tensile strain.
source: The FA-I afferent responses were best predicted by compressive strain, rather than tensile strain.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the model comparison analysis.

claim: The afferents were mostly sensitive to a particular strain orientation.
source: Moreover, the afferents were mostly sensitive to a particular strain orientation.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the orientation-dependent model analysis.

claim: The shape of the afferent receptive fields is elongated (rather than circular) and contains numerous zones of high sensitivity ('hot spots').
source: This property might be explained by the shape of the afferent receptive fields, which is elongated (rather than circular) and contains numerous zones of high sensitivity ('hot spots', Johansson, 1978; Phillips et al., 1990; Jarocka et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a fact from the literature, supported by citations.

claim: A particular arrangement of hot spots might lead to increased sensitivity to a particular strain orientation.
source: A particular arrangement of those hot spots might lead to increased sensitivity to a particular strain orientation.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism underlying the observed orientation sensitivity.

claim: Particular arrangements of hot spots enable each afferent to differentiate the orientation of edges moving across the receptive fields from the strength or the fine timing of their response.
source: Indeed, it has been demonstrated that particular arrangements enable each afferent to differentiate the orientation of edges moving across the receptive fields from the strength or the fine timing of their response (Pruszynski and Johansson, 2014; Suresh et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a fact from the literature, supported by citations.

claim: The moving strain wave related to partial slip can be seen as an edge moving across the contact area.
source: In fact, the moving strain wave related to partial slip observed in this study can be seen as an edge moving across the contact area.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental observations.

claim: The methods generate high-resolution representations of the distribution of surface strain in the contact area (2D, x and y axes) but do not allow measurements of the distribution of the deformations perpendicular to the fingertip surface inside the contact area (along the z-axis), nor outside the contact area.
source: Our methods generate high-resolution representations of the distribution of surface strain in the contact area of the fingertip (i.e., 2D, x and y axes) but do not allow measurements of the distribution of the deformations perpendicular to the fingertip surface inside the contact area (i.e., along the z-axis), nor outside the contact area.
evidence: This is a description of the limitations of the experimental methods.

claim: SA-I afferents may be more sensitive to strains perpendicular to the surface rather than tangential (planar) strains.
source: First, since SA-I afferents are known to be exquisitely sensitive to contact and contact pressure (Goodwin and Wheat, 1999; Wheat et al., 2010; Khamis et al., 2015), they may be more sensitive to the strains perpendicular to the surface, rather than the tangential (i.e., planar) strains.
evidence: This is a speculation based on known properties of SA-I afferents and the experimental findings.

claim: SA-I afferents are known to be exquisitely sensitive to contact and contact pressure.
source: First, since SA-I afferents are known to be exquisitely sensitive to contact and contact pressure (Goodwin and Wheat, 1999; Wheat et al., 2010; Khamis et al., 2015), they may be more sensitive to the strains perpendicular to the surface, rather than the tangential (i.e., planar) strains.
evidence: This is a fact from the literature, supported by citations.

claim: Tangential loading can cause a progressive redistribution of the pressure inside the contact area that will generate local vertical strains.
source: Indeed, the tangential loading can cause a progressive redistribution of the pressure inside the contact area (even if the global normal force is maintained constant) that will consequently generate 'local' vertical strains (not measured, which would be denoted 'ezz').
evidence: This is an inference about unmeasured aspects of the stimulus.

claim: SA-I shows slow firing rate variations that might be attributed to a relatively slow movement of the center of pressure during tangential loading that results in local pressure change.
source: The SA-I shows slow firing rate variations that might be well attributed to a relatively slow movement of the center of pressure during tangential loading that results in local pressure change.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism underlying SA-I responses.

claim: SA-I afferents may be sensitive to local shear (exz and eyz).
source: Another possibility is that the SA-I afferents are sensitive to local shear (which would be denoted 'exz' and 'eyz').
evidence: This is a speculation about unmeasured aspects of the stimulus that might affect SA-I responses.

claim: The fact that SA-I firing rates correlate with tangential forces supports the idea that they are sensitive to local shear.
source: The fact that their firing rates correlate with the tangential forces supports this idea, and more measurements are needed to disentangle the two possibilities.
evidence: This is an inference from the correlation analysis.

claim: Vertical strains and local shear are likely much less informative about the partial slip state of the finger than surface strains.
source: Importantly, these two other aspects of skin deformations are likely much less informative about the partial slip state of the finger; therefore, SA-I afferents are less likely to contribute to the detection of the slip events.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the nature of the unmeasured deformations.

claim: SA-I afferents are less likely to contribute to the detection of slip events.
source: Importantly, these two other aspects of skin deformations are likely much less informative about the partial slip state of the finger; therefore, SA-I afferents are less likely to contribute to the detection of the slip events.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings and speculation about unmeasured deformations.

claim: It is not surprising to observe a poor coupling between SA-II and FA-II afferent responses and the measured surface strains given the subdermal location of their terminals.
source: When considering the subdermal location of SA-II and FA-II afferent terminals, it is not surprising to observe a poor coupling between their responses and the measured surface strains.
evidence: This is an inference based on known anatomical properties and the experimental findings.

claim: The tangential speed chosen in the experiments is lower than that during normal manipulation actions.
source: The tangential speed chosen for practical reasons in our experiments is certainly lower than that during normal manipulation actions, during which much higher strain rates are probably generated.
evidence: This is a description of a limitation of the experimental design.

claim: It is unknown what the typical amplitudes of surface skin strain during manipulation are.
source: In fact, it is unknown what the typical amplitudes of surface skin strain during manipulation are.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: During active manipulation, humans typically vary the amount of grip (normal) force according to the tangential force.
source: Moreover, during active manipulation, humans typically also vary the amount of grip (normal) force according to the tangential force, while our experiment kept the normal force constant.
evidence: This is established knowledge about human manipulation behavior.

claim: It is reasonable to expect that FA-I afferents respond even more vigorously during actual manipulation.
source: Nevertheless, it is reasonable to expect that FA-I afferents respond even more vigorously during actual manipulation.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the experimental findings and considerations about natural manipulation.

claim: In this study, the partial slip phase lasts several hundreds of milliseconds, which would leave enough time for cutaneous signals to contribute to online control.
source: In this study, the partial slip phase lasts several hundreds of milliseconds, which would definitely leave enough time for cutaneous signals to contribute to online control.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data combined with inference about neural control timescales.

claim: Most surfaces encountered during natural object manipulation have frictional properties that cause stick-and-slip when the tangential load is sufficiently large.
source: Most surfaces encountered during natural object manipulation have frictional properties that cause stick-and-slip when the tangential load is sufficiently large, that is, local breaking of the bond between the surface and even a single fingerprint ridge.
evidence: This is established knowledge about surface friction properties.

claim: Stick-and-slip events were largely absent in the experiment because a flat and transparent material was used.
source: However, stick-and-slip events were largely absent in our experiment because we had to use a flat and transparent material to be able to measure skin surface deformations.
evidence: This is a description of a limitation of the experimental design.

claim: With natural material, partial slip might occur in a stepwise manner and result in readily measurable accelerations.
source: With natural material, partial slip might therefore occur in a stepwise manner and result in readily measurable accelerations (Johansson and Westling, 1984; Johansson and Westling, 1987), as opposed to a very smooth progressive wave observed in our experiments.
evidence: This is a speculation based on known properties of natural materials and citations to previous work.

claim: The patterns of deformation observed in this study will generalize in some form to other surfaces.
source: Nevertheless, while the timing might be affected, the patterns of deformation observed in their purest form in this study will generalize in some form to other surfaces and therefore the observations made in our study are likely to hold with natural materials.
evidence: This is a speculation about the generalizability of the findings.

claim: The models' R2 are relatively low for several reasons including that the models are linear whereas afferent responses are known to be more complex.
source: There are several reasons why the models' R2 are relatively low. First, the models are linear, whereas the response of tactile afferents to skin deformations is known to be far more complex than accounted for by simple linear relationships (Dong et al., 2013; Saal et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an explanation for a limitation in the modeling results, supported by citations.

claim: The inputs of the model were obtained from a single point inside the receptive field of the afferent.
source: Second, the inputs of the model were obtained from a single point inside the receptive field of the afferent.
evidence: This is a description of a limitation in the modeling approach.

claim: Human tactile afferents have complex receptive fields with multiple zones of sensitivity due to the branching of the afferent terminals in the skin.
source: Yet, we know that human tactile afferents have complex receptive fields with multiple zones of sensitivity that they owe to the branching of the afferent terminals in the skin (Johansson, 1976; Phillips et al., 1992; Pruszynski and Johansson, 2014).
evidence: This is a fact from the literature, supported by citations.

claim: The setup does not provide the ability to measure all aspects of local skin deformation, specifically deformations along the axis normal to the glass surface.
source: Finally, our setup does not provide the ability to measure all aspects of local skin deformation as discussed above; we were unable to measure deformations along the axis normal to the glass surface.
evidence: This is a description of a limitation of the experimental methods.

claim: Analyses of strain normal to the contact surface and deformations outside the contact area would require other approaches, for example, finite element analysis.
source: Analyses of strain normal to the contact surface and deformations outside the contact area would require other approaches, for example, finite element analysis.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future work to address current limitations.

claim: The ability to capture and extract very subtle mechanical phenomena arising continuously during fine manipulation is probably a key to the success of the sense of touch.
source: The ability to capture and extract very subtle mechanical phenomena arising continuously during fine manipulation is probably a key to its success.
evidence: This is a speculation about the importance of tactile sensing.

claim: Subtle skin compressions taking place in the contact area with the object's surface before slippage provide essential feedback for grasp stability.
source: We have demonstrated in this study that subtle skin compressions taking place in the contact area with the object's surface before the slippage provide essential feedback for grasp stability.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experimental findings.

claim: Estimating friction is a complex problem influenced by many factors of the object itself and by properties of the skin, some of which are constantly changing.
source: Given that estimating friction is a complex problem influenced by many factors of the object itself (texture, adhesion, hydrophilic or hydrophobic properties) and by properties of the skin (for instance, stiffness), some of which are constantly changing (e.g., humidity), the nature of this feedback and its independence from friction makes it particularly well suited for grasp stability.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the complexity of friction estimation.

claim: The nature of the feedback from FA-I afferents and its independence from friction makes it particularly well suited for grasp stability.
source: Given that estimating friction is a complex problem influenced by many factors of the object itself (texture, adhesion, hydrophilic or hydrophobic properties) and by properties of the skin (for instance, stiffness), some of which are constantly changing (e.g., humidity), the nature of this feedback and its independence from friction makes it particularly well suited for grasp stability.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings and considerations about friction complexity.

claim: Sixteen healthy human subjects (seven females; ages 19–24 years) participated in the experiment.
source: Sixteen healthy human subjects (seven females; ages 19–24 years) participated in the experiment.
evidence: This is a description of the study participants.

claim: The study was approved by the local ethics committee at Université catholique de Louvain, Brussels, Belgium.
source: Each subject provided written informed consent to the procedures, and the study was approved by the local ethics committee at the host institution (Université catholique de Louvain, Brussels, Belgium).
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval for the study.

claim: The transparent plate consisted of smooth glass and was either plain or covered with a hydrophobic coating, RainOff, reducing friction.
source: The transparent plate consisted of smooth glass and was either plain or covered with a hydrophobic coating, RainOff (Arexons, Italy) reducing friction.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental apparatus.

claim: The average RMS error of the normal force servo-control is 5% during the whole tangential loading, and average peak error is 12% or 0.5 N.
source: A custom PID controller was developed to servo-control the normal (vertical) force applied to the fingerpad by feeding back the force measurements (average RMS error is 5% during the whole tangential loading, and average peak error is 12% or 0.5 N).
evidence: This is a description of the performance of the experimental apparatus.

claim: The mean SNR across all units is 4.3 (range 2.1–7.9).
source: The mean SNR across all units is 4.3 (range 2.1–7.9).
evidence: This is a description of the quality of the electrophysiological recordings.

claim: The median effective sampling frequency across afferents was 15 Hz (Q1-3 = 3.5–38.5 Hz).
source: We found that, indeed, the stimulus did not generate effective information above 50 Hz; across afferents, median effective sampling frequency was 15 Hz (Q1-3 = 3.5–38.5 Hz).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of the afferent responses.

claim: The median number of spikes used to build the STA was 373.
source: The median number of spike used to build the STA was 373.
evidence: This is a description of the data used in the spike-triggered average analysis.

claim: The outer layer of the skin has high stiffness.
source: Besides, given the high stiffness of the outer layer of the skin (Wang and Hayward, 2007), it is reasonable to assume that the area of local patches of skin is conserved after deformation.
evidence: This is a fact from the literature, supported by a citation.

claim: It is reasonable to assume that the area of local patches of skin is conserved after deformation.
source: Besides, given the high stiffness of the outer layer of the skin (Wang and Hayward, 2007), it is reasonable to assume that the area of local patches of skin is conserved after deformation.
evidence: This is an assumption based on known material properties of skin.
